title: Human review or statistics for test items
statement: Whether a measurement test's machine-written items need a person's review before students see them, or a gate on every item plus response statistics is enough, is disputed.
example: One package's machine gate screened all 786 items, and its recheck still advised a 60-item human sample.
detail: An adversarial review of a pre-pilot reading assessment objected that no person had read its machine-written items for young students. The package answered that for a measurement instrument the load-bearing check is statistical, not editorial: a 14-dimension machine gate screens every item, misfitting items are dropped or re-estimated at calibration, and its scores carry no consequence before validation (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/PROTEST_BRIEF.md`). The recheck scored the point answered, not closed, a refusal with reasons rather than a fix, and still advised a 60-item human sample (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RECHECK_FINDINGS.md`).
against: Both sides agree that items which passed no gate may not be served: 32 items written while the gate was down were replaced (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/PROTEST_BRIEF.md`, line 67; `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/skill/SKILL.md`, line 83).

evidence.quote: For a measurement instrument, the load-bearing QC is statistical, not editorial.
Its scores carry no mastery, grade, or accountability consequence before validation — by code, not by promise.
But it is a *refusal with reasons*, not a fix
sampling remains advisable even under the §9 stance — a 60-item human sample is cheap insurance
